div.head: I Ew 1
div.ab: ⁊ ic wille, ðæt gehwilc man hæbbe his geteaman; ⁊ nan man ne ceapige butan porte, ac hæbbe þæs portgerefan gewitnesse oððe oþera ungeligenra manna, ðe man gelyfan mæge.
⁊ ic wille, þæt gehwilc man hæbbe his geteaman; ⁊ nan man ne ceapige butan porte, ac hæbbe ðæs portgerefan gewitnesse oððe oðera ungeligenra man[na], ðe man gelyfan mæge.
Et uolo, ut omnis homo habeat aduocatum suum; et nemo barganniet extra portum, sed habeat portiréue testimonium uel alterius non mendacis hominis, cui possit credi.
[Be ceapunge.] ⁊ ic wille, ðæt gehwilc man hæbbe his geteaman; ⁊ nan man ne ceapige butan porte, ac hæbbe þæs portgerefan gewitnesse oððe oþera ungeligenra manna, ðe man gelyfan mæge.

(Vom Kaufen. Ld) Und ich will, dass jedermann seinen Gewährsmann habe; und niemand kaufe ausserhalb der Stadt, sondern habe Zeugniss des Stadtvogts oder anderer wahrhaftiger Männer, denen man glauben könne.
(Of buying. Ld) And I will that everyone have his warrantor; and that no one buy outside a town, but have the witness of the town-reeve or of other truthful men whom one can believe.

And my will is that every man shall have a warrantor [to his transactions] and that no one shall buy [and sell] except in a market town; but he shall have the witness of the 'port-reeve' or of other men of credit, who can be trusted.

Cf. Gl Handel 8a. b. g; Anefang 4ff.
Wohl benutzt in II As 12. — Barganniare Romanisches Latein (Ducange), Mittelenglisch seit c. 1200 nachweisbar
Probably used in II As 12. — Barganniare is Romance Latin (Ducange), and is attested in Middle English from c. 1200

Nicht ‘des Tores’, was Schmid 643 bessert. Vgl. Gl Stadt 1. k. 15; binnan ⁊ butan porte steht völlig synonym mit burge Urk. 1067 bei Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 12. 14. [Ein zweites Masc. port heisst und stammt von porta; Earle Philol. Engl. tongue 18]. Komposita von port ‘Stadt’ s. Toller: portgeat, -gerefa, -geriht, -mann, -stræt, -wara, -weall, ferner mittel- und neuengl.: portmarsh, -meadow, -mot, -socn. — Q denkt mit portus nicht etwa an ‘Hafen’, er glossiert II As 12 dazu: civitatem. — S. Gl Vogt 3. 18

Not ‘of the gate’, a rendering which Schmid 643 corrects. Cf. Gl Stadt 1. k. 15; binnan ⁊ butan porte is used entirely synonymously with burge in a charter of 1067 in Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 12. 14. [A second masc. port means, and derives from, porta; Earle Philol. Engl. tongue 18]. For compounds of port ‘town’ see Toller: portgeat, -gerefa, -geriht, -mann, -stræt, -wara, -weall, and further, in Middle and Modern English: portmarsh, -meadow, -mot, -socn. — By portus Q is not thinking, say, of ‘harbour’; on II As 12 he glosses it: civitatem. — See Gl Vogt 3. 18
Einen Kaufzeugen (s. d. Gl 6) fordert II As 12; vielleicht daher weicht hier Q ab
II As 12 requires a witness to the purchase (see that word in Gl 6); perhaps that is why Q deviates here
i.e. the reeve in charge of a town (port). For ‘port’ see Maitland, Domesday Book and Beyond, p. 195 f. (cf. note 1 to II As. cap. 14; note 2 to II As. cap. 14 § 2).
